question: Bright-red rectal bleeding in a patient over 40 years old should never be attributed to haemorrhoids without first excluding colorectal carcinoma, regardless of whether haemorrhoids are visible on proctoscopy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is true and a vital patient-safety rule. Colorectal carcinoma and haemorrhoids commonly coexist in older patients. Visible haemorrhoids do NOT exclude a proximal cancer. Every patient over 40 with rectal bleeding must have the proximal colon evaluated.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The clinical rule from this SDL: 'never call rectal bleeding just piles without excluding colorectal cancer.' Haemorrhoids and carcinoma frequently coexist, and the visible haemorrhoid can mask a more proximal cancer. Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy is mandatory in any patient over 40 with rectal bleeding.
